candidates.title: Conceptual animation versus measured result
candidates.central_question: Did this animation happen in an experiment, or is it only showing how an idea could work?
candidates.viewer_outcome: Read the status before reading the result.
visuals_and_data: Split screen: unlabeled-looking mechanism is corrected into a visibly CONCEPTUAL diagram.
The same layout receives measured axes, workload, boundary, interval, and source locator.
Five status badges settle into the series legend and remain available as a persistent corner key.
misconceptions: Polished motion graphics are automatically experimental evidence.
caveats: A clear diagram is not evidence until its source, scope, boundary, and uncertainty are attached.
reuse_opportunities: conceptual, measured, revised, negative, and not-promoted scene status

candidates.title: Why Boolean computation matters
candidates.central_question: How do we turn a rule that sounds reasonable into something every machine must answer the same way?
candidates.viewer_outcome: The stable object is the assignment-to-output mapping, not the syntax or storage chosen later.
visuals_and_data: A concrete four-input decision rule lights its inputs and one true/false output.
The rule expands into assignment cards that become rows of an output column.
The output column fans into several possible representations, none marked as the winner.
misconceptions: Boolean computation is only about one written expression rather than the function over all assignments.
caveats: This lesson motivates exact Boolean computation; it does not establish that CM is the best representation for every task.
reuse_opportunities: why repeated exact Boolean evaluation is useful

candidates.title: Expression, truth table, and Boolean function
candidates.central_question: If two formulas look different, are they necessarily different computations?
candidates.viewer_outcome: Syntax can change while the function remains identical.
visuals_and_data: Expression tree and assignment row stay synchronized as gates evaluate.
A second differently shaped tree grows beside the first and produces the same truth column.
Both trees recede while the shared assignment-to-output mapping remains centered.
misconceptions: A changed expression tree necessarily means a changed Boolean function.
caveats: Matching one or two examples is not equivalence; the declared assignment universe must match exactly.

candidates.title: Live support versus ambient variables
candidates.central_question: Why can a six-variable table contain a function that really depends on only three variables?
candidates.viewer_outcome: Nominal width and semantic support answer different questions.
visuals_and_data: Ambient variables form an outer ring; only output-changing wires remain bright.
A fixed binding removes one axis while paired rows collapse onto identical outputs.
Nominal width and live support settle as two separate labeled counters.
misconceptions: Every named variable necessarily doubles the function's active computational support.
caveats: Smaller live support changes the active problem description, but it does not by itself select the fastest engine.

candidates.title: What a correspondence matrix is
candidates.central_question: How can one truth table become a two-dimensional object without changing a single output?
candidates.viewer_outcome: The matrix changes the layout, not the underlying Boolean function.
visuals_and_data: A sixteen-row truth table folds physically into a four-by-four matrix.
One assignment splits into row bits and column bits; two index cursors meet at its cell.
Live-support highlighting removes an inert axis while the declared ambient layout remains outlined.
misconceptions: A correspondence matrix is an unrelated numerical approximation rather than an exact truth layout.
caveats: The matrix is a dense output layout; this definition does not make it compact, a solver, or universally fast.

candidates.title: What CM does not claim to be
candidates.central_question: What goes wrong when one method name is used as the answer to three different questions?
candidates.viewer_outcome: CM is one exact representation family, not a universal answer label.
visuals_and_data: Three real task questions replace passive cards and route to visibly different artifacts.
A dense grid, SAT witness, and CM-IR DAG are aligned by requested output rather than ranked.
A universal-winner podium fractures into workload and boundary labels.
misconceptions: Calling an approach CM establishes compactness, solver behavior, or speed.
caveats: Current evidence supports scoped comparisons, not a claim that CM wins every task or boundary.

candidates.title: Explicit dense CM versus CM-IR
candidates.central_question: When a benchmark says CM, is it timing a matrix, a program graph, or a wrapper that creates both?
candidates.viewer_outcome: The matrix is an output layout; CM-IR is a program that can produce outputs.
visuals_and_data: The same expression forks into a dense grid and an interned DAG with different identity labels.
The DAG feeds point, flat/packed, and dense materialization exits; the grid remains the dense result.
Matched axes compare artifact, storage, reuse, and charged boundary without declaring a winner.
misconceptions: CM and CM-IR are two names for the same in-memory object.
caveats: A CM-IR kernel result is not automatically a dense-CM or public-wrapper result.
reuse_opportunities: dense CM versus CM-IR artifact distinction

candidates.title: CM-IR nodes, sharing, and roots
candidates.central_question: If the same Boolean subproblem appears twice, why store and compute it twice?
candidates.viewer_outcome: One node can serve several consumers without changing the function.
visuals_and_data: Two duplicate syntax branches bend toward one interned CMNode.
Reference-count and root badges appear while shared edges remain visibly distinct from tree edges.
An evaluation pulse visits each unique node once and fans the result to both consumers.
misconceptions: A CM-IR DAG must contain one independent copy of every syntactic subtree.
caveats: Sharing reduces repeated structure, but the amount of reduction depends on the expression and canonicalization rules.

candidates.title: Canonicalization, interning, and normalization
candidates.central_question: What has to happen before two differently written subexpressions can share one node?
candidates.viewer_outcome: Equivalent structure becomes reusable only after its identity is made explicit.
visuals_and_data: Messy equivalent syntax enters three labeled stations: NORMALIZE, KEY, INTERN.
Tokens reorder and flatten before a digest appears; only then does the intern table return a node.
A transformation ledger records which stage changed syntax, identity, or storage reuse.
misconceptions: Canonicalization, hashing, and interning are the same operation.
caveats: Canonicalization is implementation scoped; it does not prove a globally minimal representation.

candidates.title: CM-IR persistence and version identity
candidates.central_question: When is a graph saved yesterday still the right graph for today's source?
candidates.viewer_outcome: Persistence is an identity and invalidation contract, not merely saving bytes.
visuals_and_data: Canonical DAG becomes bytes, identity, and a versioned cache entry in one continuous chain.
A source edit travels only through affected dependency edges and converts one hit into a miss.
Reloaded graph and fresh compilation meet at an exact-output digest gate.
A collision/equal-output warning demonstrates why output equality alone is not cache authority.
misconceptions: Equal output on one check is sufficient authority to reuse an artifact from changed source.
caveats: A hash match supports identity checking; it does not by itself establish scientific truth or permit stale reuse.

candidates.title: Packed truth vectors: big integers, machine words, and masks
candidates.central_question: How can one machine operation evaluate many assignments at the same time?
candidates.viewer_outcome: Packed storage changes how outputs travel through the machine, not what outputs mean.
visuals_and_data: Truth-table outputs slide into bit positions with MSB-first ordering labeled.
One long bigint bar splits into fixed-width word lanes without changing bit identities.
A gate operates across all bits; a tail mask removes invalid high positions.
misconceptions: Packed words, CSE-flat, and a dense correspondence matrix are interchangeable representations.
caveats: Packing is an exact execution layout, not a dense CM and not evidence that words are always faster than bigint.

candidates.title: Eager and lazy CM paths
candidates.central_question: If both paths return the same output, what exactly makes one eager and the other lazy?
candidates.viewer_outcome: Eager and lazy change scheduling, not semantics.
visuals_and_data: Two synchronized timelines place identical work blocks at different stages.
Eager fills aligned regions early; lazy carries outlined placeholders until output demand.
Both paths terminate at one exact truth layout with no winner badge.
misconceptions: Lazy means no materialization work is ever performed.
caveats: The implementation distinction does not establish a universal performance ranking.

candidates.title: Pair-aware CM collapse
candidates.central_question: When can a larger expression safely collapse to one tiny row-column pair?
candidates.viewer_outcome: One live variable per axis makes the pair path possible; everything else stays on the exact fallback path.
visuals_and_data: Row and column support counters shrink independently to one and one.
The eligible axes snap into a two-by-two token tile and compute all four cases.
An ineligible third variable diverts through a clearly labeled exact fallback arrow.
misconceptions: Any subexpression with two total variables is automatically pair-eligible regardless of axis placement.
caveats: Pair eligibility is experimental and local; ineligible cases must fall back without changing semantics.

candidates.title: Hybrid versus partial-hybrid materialization
candidates.central_question: Does hybrid execution collapse the whole graph, or can it preserve structure and choose child by child?
candidates.viewer_outcome: Hybrid changes the materialization boundary; partial-hybrid changes it selectively.
visuals_and_data: A shared DAG carries a live-support heat map and explicit dispatch decisions.
Hybrid view collapses the selected whole region into one packed block.
Partial-hybrid view collapses children while the upper graph remains and feeds a no-reinflation output.
misconceptions: Hybrid and partial-hybrid are two labels for the same full-collapse behavior.
caveats: These are implemented strategies, not guarantees that one wins every support size or workload.

candidates.title: Parallel CM materialization
candidates.central_question: If rows can be computed independently, why not always send every row to another worker?
candidates.viewer_outcome: Parallelism redistributes work; it does not remove the need to count the work.
visuals_and_data: A matrix gains chunk boundaries only after minimum-work guards pass.
Ordered tiles enter worker swim lanes with stable row-index tags.
Tiles return to one exact matrix while overhead remains a separate visible band.
misconceptions: More workers necessarily make every materialization faster.
caveats: Parallelism adds scheduling and data-movement cost, so availability is not evidence of a speedup.

candidates.title: Why a raw expression tree repeats work
candidates.central_question: Why does the evaluator compute A AND B twice when both copies mean the same thing?
candidates.viewer_outcome: The raw tree shows the duplication that later comparators are designed to remove.
visuals_and_data: The repeated subtree is outlined in two positions of the syntax tree.
An evaluation pulse visits both copies and an operation counter advances twice.
The two identical result tokens hover near each other, setting up the next episode's merge.
misconceptions: Raw AST is a fair final baseline for a compiler whose competitors share repeated subexpressions.
caveats: Raw AST is an informative ablation, not the strongest comparator for a system that shares structure.

candidates.title: Common subexpression elimination in plain language
candidates.central_question: What is the simplest way to stop computing the same subtree twice?
candidates.viewer_outcome: Share identical work first; ask about flattening next.
visuals_and_data: Duplicate subtrees receive matching structural-key tags.
Their branches bend toward one shared node while both consumer edges remain.
The evaluation pulse computes S once and distributes one result token twice.
misconceptions: CSE automatically performs every normalization or associative flattening available to CM-IR.
caveats: Plain CSE shares repeats; it does not necessarily flatten an associative chain into a wider instruction.

candidates.title: Plain CSE versus sharing-aware CSE-flat
candidates.central_question: Can we widen an AND chain without tearing apart the sharing we just created?
candidates.viewer_outcome: CSE-flat strengthens plain CSE without sacrificing the sharing that made CSE useful.
visuals_and_data: Raw AST, plain CSE, and CSE-flat remain synchronized in three narrow panels.
Shared nodes carry lock icons; eligible single-consumer chains unfold into one n-ary operation.
A before/after instruction ledger attributes reductions to sharing or flattening separately.
misconceptions: CSE-flat means flatten every matching operator regardless of shared consumers.
caveats: Always-splice flattening is not the comparator contract; shared children must be preserved.

candidates.title: CM-IR versus CSE-flat: shared mechanisms and extra transformations
candidates.central_question: After CSE-flat already shares and flattens, what work is actually left for CM-IR to remove?
candidates.viewer_outcome: Common mechanisms belong to both arms; only measured deltas belong to the comparison.
visuals_and_data: A common transformation stack feeds both arms before they diverge.
A delta ledger labels each changed node as sharing, flattening, normalization, or merging.
The final graphs align by semantic node and lowered instruction rather than by method logo.
misconceptions: Every difference between CM-IR and raw AST is an advantage unique to CM-IR over CSE-flat.
caveats: A method label is not a mechanism, and one workload's residual reduction is not universal.

candidates.title: From DAGs to flat instructions: operations, storage, and execution
candidates.central_question: When someone says flat, do they mean a flattened expression, a linear instruction program, or packed bits?
candidates.viewer_outcome: Flat syntax, flat instructions, and packed storage are different stages of one execution pipeline.
visuals_and_data: DAG nodes descend into a linear postorder instruction tape with matching identity colors.
One instruction expands into several primitive-operation pulses while counters remain separate.
Slot lifetime bars end at last use and release buffers; a HYPOTHESIS badge appears over hardware traffic arrows.
CSE-flat transformation, FlatProgram, bigint bits, and word lanes settle as four noninterchangeable layers.
misconceptions: CSE-flat, FlatProgram, and word-packed execution are three names for the same artifact.
caveats: Instruction and operation counts are measured structural metrics, but hardware memory traffic remains a hypothesis unless measured directly.
reuse_opportunities: structural memory metrics versus hardware-memory hypothesis

candidates.title: Preparation, kernel, wrapper, and end-to-end time
candidates.central_question: How can a kernel be faster while the easy public call is slower?
candidates.viewer_outcome: The boundary is part of the result, not a footnote to it.
visuals_and_data: One persistent horizontal pipeline replaces separate cards for every boundary.
Colored brackets expand from kernel-only to wrapper and end-to-end scopes.
The B2/B4 kernel advantage and wrapper loss occupy different brackets simultaneously.
misconceptions: A faster compiled kernel automatically makes preparation, wrapper, and end-to-end execution faster.
caveats: Numbers from different boundaries may be shown together only when they remain visibly separate.
reuse_opportunities: preparation, kernel, wrapper, extraction, persistence, and end-to-end timing boundaries

candidates.title: How to read a CM/comparator ratio
candidates.central_question: Does a ratio below one mean faster, slower, or nothing at all?
candidates.viewer_outcome: A ratio becomes evidence only after its direction and scope are explicit.
visuals_and_data: Two labeled timers form CM/comparator and comparator/CM fractions side by side.
The same point flips around one when the ratio direction reverses.
A retained ratio appears only after workload, boundary, interval, and favorable arrow are in place.
misconceptions: Every point below one favors CM regardless of numerator, metric, or boundary.
caveats: Position and color cannot substitute for labels, scope, boundary, and uncertainty.

candidates.title: Why scopes and boundaries matter
candidates.central_question: Why can't four honest numbers be averaged into one honest winner?
candidates.viewer_outcome: Honest evidence gets narrower before it gets stronger.
visuals_and_data: A matrix uses workloads as rows and timing boundaries as columns; results occupy different cells.
A pooling funnel rejects cards with mismatched output, boundary, machine, or dependence structure.
Allowed wording updates as the viewer drags a scope bracket across cells.
misconceptions: All CM/comparator ratios estimate one underlying universal performance number.
caveats: B2/B4, EPFL, preparation, kernel, and wrapper evidence remain separate when their scopes differ.

candidates.title: Reuse and break-even economics
candidates.central_question: How many evaluations does it take to repay a more expensive compilation?
candidates.viewer_outcome: Preparation is a debt; reuse determines whether the debt is ever repaid.
visuals_and_data: Two cumulative-cost lines grow from different preparation intercepts.
A reuse slider moves the crossing point or reveals that no crossing exists.
The retained EPFL distribution separates finite break-even cases from 55 never cases.
misconceptions: Any per-evaluation advantage guarantees a finite and useful break-even point.
caveats: Some retained cases never break even, and a modeled crossing is not an end-to-end deployment guarantee.

candidates.title: Corrected B2/B4 V3 kernel result
candidates.central_question: What survives after the comparator, balancing, exactness, and boundary problems are corrected?
candidates.viewer_outcome: The bare-kernel result survived correction; the universal speed claim did not.
visuals_and_data: Comparator ladder locks CSE-flat as primary while raw AST moves to an ablation lane.
A formula-balanced interval plot constructs overall and k=16 points progressively.
Kernel and wrapper rows stay aligned but cannot merge; their favorable directions visibly differ.
misconceptions: The corrected kernel ratio establishes that the public CM API is faster end to end.
caveats: These estimates are conditional on this workload, machine, run, comparator, and boundary.

candidates.title: Three-pod B2/B4 replication
candidates.central_question: What does three-machine agreement add, and what does it still not prove?
candidates.viewer_outcome: Replication adds another scope; it does not erase scope.
visuals_and_data: Four machine columns build independently from verified raw results.
Overall and k=16 points remain paired within each column.
A POOL button is visibly refused because the design lacks a declared between-machine model.
misconceptions: Three similar pod ratios can automatically be averaged into the local study's confidence interval.
caveats: The three pod values are descriptive; they are not a predeclared pooled confidence interval.

candidates.title: EPFL AND/INV parity and its mechanism
candidates.central_question: What happens when the strong comparator has already captured every associative merge available in the circuit?
candidates.viewer_outcome: No extra structural reduction meant no accepted kernel advantage on this workload.
visuals_and_data: A circuit cone zooms to binary gates and semantic support.
Matched lowered instruction streams align one for one and lock both mechanism counters at 1.000.
The timing interval settles across the parity line while preparation remains on a separate cost band.
misconceptions: EPFL parity proves CM and CSE-flat are universally identical on every workload.
caveats: EPFL parity is scoped to these cones and does not contradict the distinct B2/B4 kernel result.

candidates.title: Why width alone did not select the engine
candidates.central_question: If machine words sound natural above a certain width, why not switch at that number?
candidates.viewer_outcome: Width informs the decision; it does not make the decision alone.
visuals_and_data: A width axis routes cases toward bigint or word lanes.
Per-case regret bars reveal one severe counterexample that aggregate medians would hide.
The promotion gate turns red and the deployed-rule box remains unchanged.
misconceptions: A support-width cutoff can universally choose between bigint and word-packed evaluation.
caveats: The focused study reused validation and failed its gate; it did not justify a universal width threshold.

candidates.title: Truth digests, alternating schedules, clustering, and intervals
candidates.central_question: What can make a precise timing number wrong even when the timer itself is accurate?
candidates.viewer_outcome: Each protocol guard earns one part of the claim and no more.
visuals_and_data: Four red validity threats enter four lanes and meet distinct guards.
A timing ribbon alternates arm order while exact output digests remain outside the timed bracket.
Repeated rows gather into formula clusters before resampling and interval construction.
A final audit card lists which threats are controlled and which uncertainties remain out of scope.
misconceptions: Passing exact-output equality automatically removes timing-order, dependence, and external-validity problems.
caveats: The retained interval models formula clustering within the declared run; it does not model every machine or future workload.

candidates.title: Why one blended fastest-method chart is dishonest
candidates.central_question: What had to be hidden to make one method look fastest everywhere?
candidates.viewer_outcome: The honest answer is conditional because the actual tasks are different.
visuals_and_data: A glossy three-place podium appears with method logos but no task labels.
Missing labels return as physical layers and pull results into different grid cells.
The podium dissolves into an animated decision map with no universal top cell.
misconceptions: A blended chart can summarize unlike measurement boundaries without changing their meaning.
caveats: Current CM evidence deliberately contains a kernel advantage, a parity workload, and a slower wrapper.

candidates.title: How an audit changed the headline
candidates.central_question: Did the audit erase the old work, or did it change what the work was allowed to claim?
candidates.viewer_outcome: A good audit changes the claim without pretending the history never happened.
visuals_and_data: A source-to-claim timeline preserves older artifacts but marks superseded wording.
Four audit changes enter as patches and update comparator, exactness, weighting, and boundary nodes.
EPFL parity, B2/B4 kernel reduction, and wrapper loss remain as separate current leaves.
misconceptions: A correction either invalidates every earlier result or can be ignored as a wording-only change.
caveats: The current conclusion is not one replacement ratio: EPFL, B2/B4 kernel, and the wrapper remain separate results.

candidates.title: CM, CSE, BitSet, BDD, SAT, Espresso, and SymPy: different questions
candidates.central_question: Which tool is best—the one that returns every output, one witness, a canonical graph, or a smaller expression?
candidates.viewer_outcome: Tools become comparable only after they are asked to do the same job.
visuals_and_data: A task question enters a radial router whose exits are labeled by returned artifact, not method prestige.
Each tool produces a visibly different object: matrix, DAG/program, packed vector, BDD, witness, minimized expression, or symbolic expression.
Cost bands for build, query, extraction, and reuse appear only on relevant routes.
Two example requests take different branches and settle side by side without a podium.
misconceptions: CM, BDD, SAT, Espresso, and SymPy are interchangeable engines for one common output contract.
caveats: This map explains interfaces and retained evidence; it is not a full tutorial or universal benchmark for every tool.

candidates.title: Configuration and feature-model workloads
candidates.central_question: What changes when the rule set is almost the same tomorrow but not byte-for-byte identical?
candidates.viewer_outcome: Configuration performance lives in the sequence of related questions, not one isolated formula.
visuals_and_data: Feature tree and constraint graph respond to interactive-looking toggles with exact conflict paths.
Three source revisions align as a diff; only affected graph regions and identities change color.
Cold, cached, and invalidated paths share one timeline with all validation work charged.
A task router sends enumeration, point checks, and revision reuse to different output contracts.
misconceptions: Equal output on adjacent feature-model revisions proves that cached structure is valid.
caveats: The retained studies are bounded revision and task cases; they do not establish universal CM dominance for configuration systems.

candidates.title: Circuit workloads: structure, truth, and exact controls
candidates.central_question: When a circuit has thousands of gates, what exact function is one output cone asking us to compute?
candidates.viewer_outcome: Measure the function of the cone you actually selected, not the size of the circuit around it.
visuals_and_data: A full circuit fades while one output cone and its fan-in remain bright.
Semantic-support testing removes an ambient input that cannot influence the cone output.
Matched gate graph, lowered instructions, and exact digest remain synchronized.
The conceptual cone hands off to a separately badged retained EPFL panel.
misconceptions: Nominal circuit size directly determines the semantic support and strongest evaluation method for every cone.
caveats: The accepted parity result belongs to selected EPFL AND/INV cones, not to all circuits or all tasks.

candidates.title: Policy and rule systems with related revisions
candidates.central_question: If two policy versions share most of their rules, how much work can be reused safely?
candidates.viewer_outcome: Safe rule reuse is an end-to-end identity and cost problem.
visuals_and_data: A policy graph grows from role, region, resource, and risk predicates into one decision.
Three revisions align; unchanged subgraphs remain shared while one clause and its dependents invalidate.
A proved-rule certificate travels with the rewrite and returns to exact fallback on refusal.
An overhead ledger prevents the operation reduction from becoming an automatic speedup badge.
misconceptions: A rewrite that reduces expression operations necessarily improves the complete policy request.
caveats: More exact rewrites or fewer operations do not guarantee a faster overhead-inclusive policy task.

candidates.title: Which representation should I try?
candidates.central_question: What should you ask before choosing CM, CSE-flat, packed evaluation, BDD, or SAT?
candidates.viewer_outcome: The right representation is conditional on the task you actually need to complete.
visuals_and_data: An animated decision tree asks one concrete question per branch and shows why each answer matters.
Two persistent workload tokens traverse different branches and retain their reasoning trail.
Unsupported evidence ends at a MEASURE/ABSTAIN node rather than a guessed winner.
misconceptions: One property such as width or nominal variable count can universally select the best representation.
caveats: The decision flow narrows eligible approaches; it does not replace measurement on a new workload.

candidates.title: What the CRSE research program asks
candidates.central_question: Can a learned system suggest useful Boolean structure without becoming the authority on correctness?
candidates.viewer_outcome: CRSE studies when guidance helps while exact computation remains the safety authority.
visuals_and_data: An 18-track program map groups routing, recognition, rewrites, exact dispatch, guidance, and negative controls.
Matrix MLP, CNN, source-DAG GNN, fused, and retrieval tokens reach separate generated, retrieval, and EPFL outcome panels.
Proposal and exact-verification lanes use distinct colors and never merge before acceptance.
A four-stage gate separates exactness, measured benefit, transfer, and promotion for every later milestone.
misconceptions: A milestone that passes exact verification automatically proves learned generalization or production readiness.
caveats: CRSE is a project label in the authoritative sources; no production model or invented acronym expansion is allowed.

candidates.title: C2 variable-size decomposition: exact control, learned failure
candidates.central_question: What if the exact detector works perfectly but the learned detector fails on a larger size?
candidates.viewer_outcome: Exact recognition advanced; learned transfer did not.
visuals_and_data: A small truth layout splits into row and column factors and recomposes through an exact witness gate.
Training and held-out size lanes never visually overlap.
Exact-control and learned-model result cards settle independently; only the learned promotion gate fails.
misconceptions: A perfect exact control implies that the trained learner has discovered the same transferable rule.
caveats: The exact detector's success does not rescue the failed learned size-transfer criterion.

candidates.title: C3-C5 natural cuts: improvements without held-out promotion
candidates.central_question: Can better natural data and a better readout turn local improvement into a reliable held-out cut?
candidates.viewer_outcome: The learned path improved, but the exact control remained the accepted path.
visuals_and_data: A milestone timeline adds one methodological change at C3, C4, and C5 without resetting earlier evidence.
Matched positive/negative graph pairs expose why superficial graph cues are insufficient.
Predicted cut edges pass through an exact witness gate before acceptance.
Confirmatory and held-out panels remain side by side, with cost charged below both.
misconceptions: Any increase in confirmatory accuracy is sufficient evidence of held-out generalization.
caveats: Improvement on confirmatory circuits did not satisfy the required held-out promotion or cost criteria.

candidates.title: C6-C8 exact source ANF: packed cores and transfer
candidates.central_question: What can advance when a deterministic exact core improves but one frozen gate still misses?
candidates.viewer_outcome: Exact transfer was stronger than any universal backend ranking.
visuals_and_data: A source DAG becomes a coefficient map and then a packed integer with bit identities visible.
Core, gate, and production-path cards use separate status badges.
Windows, independent Yosys source, and Linux lanes compare exact identities before any timing.
A backend portfolio triangle shifts by sparse median, tail protection, and machine without choosing one universal vertex.
misconceptions: A packed-core improvement proves that packed ANF is the fastest exact representation on every source and machine.
caveats: Exact identity transferred; the fastest set, packed, or bitset representation did not become universal.
reuse_opportunities: C8 Linux exact transfer and backend sensitivity

candidates.title: C9-C11 exact routing: static trees, guarded restart, and one-pass conversion
candidates.central_question: Can an exact router solve a catastrophic tail and still be the wrong default?
candidates.viewer_outcome: C9-C11 explain why C12 needed a robust guarded policy rather than a more confident universal router.
visuals_and_data: A fixed set/packed/bitset arm rail stays visible beneath all three experimental routers.
The C9 tree chooses an exact arm, then its held-out cost token lands below the profitability gate.
C10's product counter triggers a guarded restart while median and p95 gauges move independently.
C11 transforms one live set prefix into packed bits without a second DAG traversal, but its complete-cost bar still misses one.
misconceptions: Eliminating duplicate prefix work or improving p95 automatically makes an exact router profitable on sparse cases.
caveats: All three preserved exact outputs; none beat the best fixed arm on every retained split, so tail protection and median profitability remain separate.

candidates.title: C12-C16 exact dispatch, tail guards, and GF(2) artifacts
candidates.central_question: Can one exact system protect catastrophic tails without slowing every sparse case?
candidates.viewer_outcome: The later C milestones advance a cross-machine exact guarded portfolio, not one universal engine.
visuals_and_data: An exact dispatcher moves one task token through fixed arms while a fallback rail remains visible.
Latency-tail and sparse-throughput gauges expose why C13 needs the C14 task guard.
A GF(2) matrix decomposes into reconstructible component/rank/cofactor/Kronecker artifacts.
Sixty-four partition outlines share one layout; four selected descriptors become solid artifacts before matched local/Linux evidence panels settle.
misconceptions: Passing a Linux confirmation makes the screened path a universal per-case or cross-family winner.
caveats: C16 passed the corrected Linux second-machine gate, but one tiny local case regressed and a fresh non-XOR-heavy family remains untested.

candidates.title: C17-C20 exact policies: dispatch, transfer, fitting, and compilation
candidates.central_question: How can the same exact policy look strong in aggregate and still fail the rule needed for safe deployment?
candidates.viewer_outcome: C17-C20 turn a promising exact arm into a better-understood policy boundary, not a promoted universal dispatcher.
visuals_and_data: Two exact CM/GF(2) arm lanes feed one artifact-identity checker while a separately metered C17 wrapper exposes aggregate, slow-tail, and minimum gates.
A frozen-policy seal crosses from the Yosys-derived lane to a 73-cone VTR source map; exact matches settle before the one-round timing distribution appears.
A source-cluster wall partitions 96 LogikBench cones into development, validation, and confirmation without any cluster crossing the boundaries.
The fitted C19 tree visibly collapses to one screened leaf; feature and tree overhead remain highlighted as removable work rather than mathematical evidence.
A compiler folds that leaf into a direct selector, then nine retrospective timing rings replace the earlier one-round outlier without changing the production lock.
misconceptions: The C20 repeated-tail pass retroactively makes the C18 single-round scout fresh confirmation or promotes the policy.
caveats: C19 supplies fresh source-cluster confirmation on one machine, while C20 is a retrospective same-machine replay, so neither licenses a universal production rule.

candidates.title: C21-C22 task-matched GF(2): seven methods and a frozen source-packed portfolio
candidates.central_question: What changes when seven methods must return the best exact artifact instead of any reconstructible factor?
candidates.viewer_outcome: C21-C22 justify a guarded source-packed candidate for fresh testing, not a learned router or deployed default.
visuals_and_data: One exhaustive-best artifact silhouette sits above seven method lanes; each lane must deliver the same identity before its timing cell unlocks.
A stacked whole-task ledger separates input decode, representation, proposal, exact completion, checking, cleanup, and wrapper cost for every method.
The source-packed lane forks into representation and proposal signals: ten proposal tokens advance, eighty-six abstain, and all ninety-six still enter screened completion.
Best-fixed, width-rule, and per-case-oracle bars expose only a narrow remaining routing interval before decision overhead is charged.

The C22 portfolio contract connects source-packed screened selection to exhaustive advice-off/refusal fallback and a parallel shadow identity checker; the fresh-evidence cell remains empty and labeled pending.
misconceptions: Because source-packed ANF was the fastest fixed arm, its component proposal usually pruned the exact search or C22 is already production-ready.
caveats: C21 is retrospective one-machine evidence, and C22 is implementation readiness without fresh timing, so the narrow source-packed lead is not a production claim.

candidates.title: C23 fresh Yosys transfer: exact confirmation without routing headroom
candidates.central_question: Does a fresh source family turn the narrow C21 winner into a deployable routing rule?
candidates.viewer_outcome: C23 strengthens the fixed exact portfolio evidence while making another learned router less compelling, not more.
visuals_and_data: A two-axis evidence map separates new source families from a new machine; C23 advances only along the source-family axis.
The original support-3-to-10 corpus hits a red task-contract boundary above six, is retained as incomplete, and becomes a verified support-3-to-6 v2 freeze with prior-overlap filters visible.
Forty-eight function tokens from eight Yosys generator families pass independent scalar-oracle and prior-truth gates before entering the unchanged seven-lane task table.
Seven aligned cost lanes end at one exhaustive-best artifact identity; representation, proposal, completion, checking, cleanup, and wrapper bands remain separately labeled.
Packed source ANF, screened CM, and compiled screened CM bars settle almost together while per-case regret markers and a thin oracle-headroom bracket keep the production lock closed.
misconceptions: Because C23 uses fresh Yosys families and packed source ANF wins in aggregate, the result is already cross-machine proof or a production routing policy.
caveats: The fixed paths transfer, but the best two are separated by only 0.62%, the oracle offers only 4.7% pre-router headroom, and compiled execution still regresses on individual cases.

candidates.title: Milestones D-D7: task routing, proved rules, caching, and normalization
candidates.central_question: What happens when exact routing and rewriting are judged by the complete task rather than their inner kernel?
candidates.viewer_outcome: The system became more exact and accountable faster than it became profitable.
visuals_and_data: Four task tokens traverse separate cost pipelines rather than one blended benchmark.
A rule-pack timeline adds proof rows, deterministic priority, cache identity, and gates at D2-D4.
Natural incidence heatmaps and revision diffs ground D5-D6 in retained workloads.
A bounded normalization loop shows strict decrease, termination, extra reductions, and charged loss.
misconceptions: A proved rewrite or cache hit is automatically beneficial after its matching and validation costs are charged.
caveats: Exactness and engineering completion do not guarantee overhead-inclusive profitability.
reuse_opportunities: D5-D7 natural incidence, revisions, and normalization

candidates.title: D8 Linux confirmation: exact but unprofitable
candidates.central_question: Can an experiment reproduce perfectly and still fail its reason for deployment?
candidates.viewer_outcome: D8 is an exact engineering success and a profitability failure at the same time.
visuals_and_data: Windows and Linux lanes share frozen package, input, rule, and digest identities.
Exactness and rule-incidence checks turn green in both lanes.
Profitability arrows point in opposite directions and the promotion gate remains closed.
misconceptions: Reproducing exact outputs and rule counts is sufficient to promote a performance optimization.
caveats: Exact transfer passed, but profitability did not; the negative result is the final promotion authority.

candidates.title: D9 abstention policy: safe, charged, not promoted
candidates.central_question: If a policy avoids every bad rewrite, has it succeeded?
candidates.viewer_outcome: A safe no-op is not free, and its cost belongs in the deployment decision.
visuals_and_data: A two-gate policy separates applicability from expected gain.
All 33 workload tokens return to exact no-rewrite fallback for different documented reasons.
An overhead meter continues accumulating during abstention and closes the promotion gate.
misconceptions: An all-abstain policy is automatically equivalent in cost to having no policy.
caveats: D9 selected the faster fixed arm correctly but remained slower after advice overhead, so no policy was promoted.

candidates.title: D10 indexed rule execution: richer exact rules, negative whole-path economics
candidates.central_question: Can a much better-engineered exact rule system still lose to doing nothing?
candidates.viewer_outcome: D10 advanced the exact engine while retaining no rewrite as the economic control.
visuals_and_data: A rule index narrows candidate nodes before four rule-family matchers activate.
Accepted rewrites carry proof, decrease, source, and cache-identity tags through execution.
A whole-path ledger shows structural reductions and exact replay alongside larger total overhead.
misconceptions: Indexed matching guarantees that a larger exact rule pack repays its execution overhead.
caveats: More rule families and safer execution did not satisfy the retained whole-path profitability criterion.

candidates.title: E1-E2 exact BDD and SAT guidance: task-aware advice with fallback
candidates.central_question: Should one advisor choose the same BDD order and SAT lifecycle for every question about a Boolean function?
candidates.viewer_outcome: Task-aware advice is useful only while exact construction, checking, and fallback stay in charge.
visuals_and_data: One function produces differently shaped BDDs as the variable order ribbon changes.
Objective tabs switch between nodes, build, restriction, and equivalence without pooling them.
Expression-to-CNF animation feeds fresh, assumption-session, and miter solver lanes.
Advice controls a route selector but exact BDD/SAT artifacts and fallback remain visually downstream and authoritative.
misconceptions: One learned policy can optimize BDD size, build time, restrictions, SAT, and equivalence as one common objective.
caveats: The retained learned advice did not establish a general timing win, and solver/BDD results answer different output contracts.

candidates.title: How a video is bound to source hashes
candidates.central_question: If one evidence file changes, how do we know which sentence, scene, and rendered chapter are stale?
candidates.viewer_outcome: Reproducibility is a connected chain of identities, evidence, and approvals.
visuals_and_data: A provenance graph grows source -> locator -> claim -> bible -> script -> storyboard -> render job -> output -> release.
One source hash changes and red invalidation travels only along dependent edges.
Content approval and RunPod authorization appear as two separate locks over different artifact sets and effects.
A final reproducibility card lists exact paths, hashes, and commands without exposing a secret.
misconceptions: A valid SHA-256 alone proves the underlying scientific claim and authorizes its remote production.
caveats: Hash identity supports reproducibility and invalidation, but it does not establish scientific truth or authorize cloud spending.
